technical-data.invention-title: ALKALINE CELLS HAVING A CONDUCTIVE METAL LAYER ON A CATHODE CONTAINER AND PROCESS FOR MAKING SUCH
PILES ALCALINES POSSEDANT UNE COUCHE METALLIQUE CONDUCTRICE SUR UN BOITIER CATHODIQUE ET LEUR PROCEDE DE FABRICATION

nplcit.text: DATABASE WPI Section Ch, Week 197721 Derwent Publications Ltd., London, GB; Class L03, AN 1977-37378Y XP002149630 -& JP 52 048021 A (TOSHIBA RAY O VAC CO), 16 April 1977 (1977-04-16)
PATENT ABSTRACTS OF JAPAN vol. 1997, no. 02, 28 February 1997 (1997-02-28) -& JP 08 264193 A (MATSUSHITA ELECTRIC IND CO LTD), 11 October 1996 (1996-10-11) cited in the application

abstract.p: The present invention is a process for producing a silver layer, in situ, on an internal wall of a cathode container of an alkaline cell and the alkaline cell produced by the process. In the process a silver compound is dissolved in the cathode, which is in contact with the metal container of the cell, and silver ions diffuse through the cathode and displace metal on the inside surface of the container to coat the container surface with silver.

L'invention concerne un procédé servant à fabriquer une couche d'argent in situ sur la paroi intérieure du boîtier cathodique d'une pile alcaline et pile alcaline fabriquée au moyen de ce procédé. Ce dernier consiste à dissoudre un composé d'argent dans la cathode, qui est en contact avec le boîtier métallique de la pile, ce qui provoque la diffusion des ions argent à travers la cathode et le déplacement du métal sur la surface intérieure du boîtier afin d'en revêtir la surface par de l'argent.

description.p: ALKALINE CELLS HAVINGA CONDUCTIVEMETALLAYERONA CATHODE CONTAINERANDPROCESS FORMAKINGSUCH

The invention relates to an assembled electrochemical cell, wherein the surface of the container adjacent the electrode is coated with a layer of a metal which is more electropositive than the metallic material of the container, and to processes for producing such cells.

Alkaline cells are well known in the art and generally employ a zinc anode, a manganese dioxide cathode and an aqueous solution of potassium hydroxide as the electrolyte. In conventional alkaline cells, the manganese dioxide is shielded from atmosphere (air) through seal means. These cells are readily commercially available for industrial and home applications.

Cathode containers and collectors for alkaline cells have used steel as the material for the container. The surface iron of the container oxidises to a protective coating in high concentration aqueous potassium hydroxide electrolyte. However, this iron oxide coating is not a good electron conductor, and the thicker it gets the higher the resistance. Nickel is even worse than iron, in that the oxide is an even poorer electron conductor. However, iron- nickel alloys are better than iron or nickel alone, and an alloy of cobalt with nickel and iron is better than iron or iron-nickel. All the metal coatings show an increase in contact resistance with time as the oxide thickness builds up.

It has long been recognised that the nature of the contact between the container and the positive electrode is an important factor in cell design. It is also a fact that, in order to achieve maximum power output in a cell requires maximum amounts of the active components to be assembled in the cell, thereby militating against the use of bulky materials.
Experiments with container coatings have been performed by many researchers, and one favoured container coating was a mixture of manganese nitrate, electrolytic manganese dioxide, graphite and water, baked at 350°C to convert the manganese nitrate to MnO2. The presently preferred conductive coating for containers is a graphite paint, comprising a 5 suspension of a binder and graphite powder in a liquid carrier. The paint is applied by spraying, swabbing, brushing, etc., onto the surface to be coated. When the liquid carrier evaporates, the graphite particles, adhered to each other and to the metal surface by the binder, remain on the surface. In any such coating, it is important that the volume percent of the binder should be only adequate to bind the graphite, given that the binder is usually an 0 insulator, and excess binder will electrically isolate the graphite particles.

Inherently, any coating added to the container surface before the positive electrode is inserted into or formed within the container will be subject to abrasion damage by the electrode material. This is a problem with graphite coatings, which are easily scraped off by 5 engagement with the positive electrode.

Japanese Patent Application No. 8-264193 discloses an alkaline manganese battery having a positive electrode, which contains manganese dioxide and a carbon material, this electrode being tightly contained in a container made of metallic material. A conductor o film, containing a material selected from the group comprising an oxide of silver or silver and nickel and a binder, is sprayed on the contacting surfaces of the positive electrode container and the positive electrode. However, this coating is also easily scraped or peeled off. In addition, the process disclosed in this reference requires a step of spraying the interior surface of the container, and the sprayed-on material must further be dried before the 5 positive electrode can be inserted or formed within the container. Not only that, but the amounts of silver required are large because of the method of application. There is a further problem, in that these large amounts of silver oxide are soluble in the electrolyte, and some silver ions may migrate through the separator to the anode and react with the active anode material to generate hydrogen gas. Silver ions may also migrate to the separator and cause o short circuits during discharge of the cell.
We have found that sprayed-on conductive coatings, such as graphite or silver with a binder, are also prone to de-laminate from the can in situ, resulting in drastic performance reductions. The level of de-lamination does not need to be pronounced in order to produce these performance reductions. Small separation distances between the coating and the container allow capillary convection of electrolyte to produce a sandwich-like structure incapable of effective electron transfer. The sandwich structure (de-laminated coating on one side, electrolyte in the centre and the can surface on the other side) acts as a very effective electrical insulator, much like the heat insulation afforded by a doubly glazed window. The stagnant electrolyte between the coating and the can surface prevents electron transfer between these two surfaces.
Thus, there is a need for an effective, conductive coating for the cathode container which at least partly overcomes the above-identified problems.

We have now, surprisingly, found that compounds of highly electropositive metallic elements which are soluble in the electrolyte are capable of depositing a layer of the metal on the inside of the cathode container, in situ, and prior to any discharge by the end user.

Thus, in a first aspect, the present invention provides an assembled, undischarged electrochemical cell comprising electrolyte, an electrode and a container therefor, wherein the surface of the container adjacent the electrode is coated with a layer of a metal which is more electropositive than the metallic material of the container, characterised in that the metal layer is generated by a solute of the metal in the electrolyte. The electrode is preferably the cathode. Unless otherwise apparent, reference herein to the cathode shall be taken as reference to the electrode, as defined above.
By "undischarged" is meant a level of charge in the cell which a battery manufacturer is prepared to sell such cells on a commercial basis.

It will be appreciated that the metal may be any that suitable metal, provided that it serves to facilitate contact between the container and the cathode. The metal is suitably silver, but any metal than can form a compound soluble in the electrolyte and from which
solution is able to electrochemically deposit a layer of the metal on the container, without a current needing to be passed, is suitable.

Likewise, the nature of the compound of the metal to form the solute is not an essential feature of the invention. All that is necessary is for the compound to be soluble in sufficient quantity in the electrolyte to be able to electrochemically deposit the metal.

It will be appreciated that the metal is suitably chosen to be more electropositive than the metal constituent of the container, and it is advantageous that the electrode potential difference between the two is significant. Again, silver is generally the metal of choice.
It is particularly advantageous that the metal layer be formed in situ, to avoid the major problems associated with maintaining the integrity of the layer during assembly.

In an alternative aspect, the present invention provides a process for the preparation of an electrochemical cell comprising an electrolyte, an electrode and a container therefor made of a metallic material, the process comprising dissolving a compound of a metal more electropositive than the container in the electrolyte in a sufficient quantity that the surface of the container in contact with the cathode becomes coated with the metal by means of an electrochemical equilibrium reaction at the surface of the container.

It will be appreciated that the amount of metal compound should be at least sufficient to generate a monoatomic layer of the metal inside the can. An excess over this amount will normally be preferred, in order to ensure an efficient layer be formed. The amount used will also be determined by economic factors.

The present invention further provides a process of assembling the components of an electrochemical cell comprising the steps of: a. preparing - an electrode comprising an electrochemically active material, an electrolyte comprising a salt and a solvent, an electrically conductive container having a wall with an inner surface comprising a first metal, and
a compound of a second metal more electropositive than the first metal; b. assembling the electrode, electrolyte and metal compound within the container so the electrode is in contact with the wall of the container, the electrolyte is mixed with the electrode, and the electrolyte is in contact with both the metal compound and the inner surface of the container; c. dissolving the metal compound in the electrolyte; and d. producing an electrically conductive layer of the second metal on the inner surface of the wall of the container.

The present invention further provides a process for making an electrochemical cell having a cell container with a wall, a positive electrode that contacts the container wall, a negative electrode and an electrolyte, the process comprising: a. adding an amount of a silver compound to the cell; and b. replacing at least a portion of material of the container wall in contact with the positive electrode with silver to form a layer of silver, without discharging the cell.
In a further aspect, the present invention provides an electrochemical cell produced using a process of the invention.

The present invention further relates to an electrochemical cell comprising a first electrode, a second electrode, a separator between the first and second electrodes and an electrolyte within a cell container having an inner surface, wherein at least a portion of the inner surface of the container contains a layer of silver, and wherein the inner surface of the container is not coated with silver prior to combining the container with other cell components.

The invention also relates to an electrochemical cell having an electrode and an electrolyte positioned within a conductive housing, wherein the conductive housing comprises an internal wall positioned adjacent the electrode, and the internal wall of the container contains a layer of silver produced in situ in the undischarged cell.
It is an advantage of the present invention that there is provided a process for assembling an alkaline manganese dioxide cell that is cost effective and allows easy assembly.

It is an advantage of the present invention that, where silver is used, then only a minimum amount of silver needs to be used. In addition, it is now possible to provide a conductive surface for the positive electrode container which allows for the elimination of any cladding of the container.
It is possible for these advantages to be realised without the addition of more process steps than used in the art.

It has been discovered that a small amount of silver oxide, for example, mixed with a manganese dioxide containing mix of an alkaline-manganese cell will provide service advantages over the use of manganese dioxide alone. Silver oxide (both Ag2O and AgO) is soluble in an aqueous potassium hydroxide and other alkaline solutions suitable for use as an electrolyte in an alkaline-manganese-zinc cell. Silver halide, such as silver chloride, will be converted to silver oxide in an aqueous potassium hydroxide electrolyte solution and is also suitable for use in cells with alkaline electrolytes. Silver halide is also soluble in an acidic electrolyte solution, making it suitable for use in cells with such electrolytes as well.

Although the present invention is particularly relevant to alkaline cells, it is not so limited, and is applicable to all relevant metals, particularly all silver compounds (including, but not limited to, silver oxides and silver salts) soluble in the appropriate electrolytic solutions. The dissolution of silver oxide, for example, results in a thin silver layer being deposited on the wall of the container that contacts the positive electrode. The minimum amount of silver compound necessary is that amount which results in a single atomic layer of residue on the container. Compounds of other metals that are more electropositive than the metal of the inside container surface (e.g., iron, nickel and/or cobalt) are also suitable for use in the present invention, provided that they are soluble in the electrolyte solution.
With cells made with silver oxide substituted for 4.4% of the manganese dioxide, the cells gave an increase in performance and a higher short circuit amperage than would have been expected if the only contribution from the silver oxide was as a depolariser. Although discharging the cell would reduce silver oxide to metallic silver, thereby improving conductivity and short circuit amperage, reduction of silver oxide would not be expected in an undischarged cell. In general, it appears that, since silver oxide is soluble in an aqueous electrolyte of potassium hydroxide, and that silver is more electropositive than iron, nickel and cobalt, then silver displaces these metals on the surface of the can which is in contact with the silver oxide/electrolyte solution. 0

As confirmation, silver oxide was dissolved in a 9N potassium hydroxide solution left in an AA (LR6) container overnight. After decanting the solution, a silver layer was left on the wall of the container. Cells made from these containers, showed a higher short circuit amperage and gave increased service to 1.0 V on 2.0 A continuous tests. 5

The amount of silver oxide required is preferably an effective amount to provide a silver layer on the internal wall of the cell's container. For most alkaline cell applications, the minimum amount of silver oxide to be incorporated in the positive electrode mix can be that amount needed to form a monoatomic layer of silver covering that portion of the o container that will be in contact with the positive electrode. This corresponds with a silver oxide amount of about 0.00003 weight percent of the active amount in the positive electrode. If the silver oxide concentration is too large, then this can result in the silver plating onto the separator, causing short circuiting. The preferred range is between about 0.01 weight percent and about 0J weight percent, and most preferably between about 0.02 5 weight percent and about 0.05 weight percent of the active material in the positive electrode.

It will be appreciated that the terms "silver" and "silver oxide" are used interchangeably herein with any other term relating to an appropriate electropositive metal and any suitable compound thereof, as defined herein, respectively. 0

The minimum thickness of the silver layer of the present invention should be that corresponding to the atomic diameter of the silver atom, that is 2.88 Angstroms. Generally,
the less silver oxide that is added, the less cost added to the finished cell. The silver layer thickness is preferably about 0.0005 μm to about 3 μm; more preferably between about 0.007 μm to about 1 μm; and most preferably between 0.0009 μm and 0.001 μm.

5 A conductive material, such as graphite, is generally used in the positive electrode mix to provide electrical contact to the positive electrode container. Graphite is an inert material in the cell and occupies space that could be used for the active components of the cell. A benefit of the invention is that the addition of silver oxide to the positive electrode mix provides electrical contact via the silver layer between the container and the positive 0 electrode, so the amount of graphite in the positive electrode mix can be reduced. This makes more volume available for the active components of the cell which results in an increase in the discharge capacity of the cell.

The electrochemical cells of the invention can comprise an alkaline electrolyte, a 5 silver oxide-containing cathode and an anode arranged in a sealed container in a manner effective to provide electrochemical energy, i.e. when the cell is placed in a circuit, electrochemical energy is provided to the circuit. The cells have terminals of opposite polarity. One terminal is in contact with the cathode and the other is in contact with the anode. The cell is sealed in a manner effective to contain the cell components in the o container under conditions of transport and use and to prevent air from entering the cell.

The cell construction can include a metallic container suitably constructed of steel or other metal and can be plated in whole or in part. The plating can consist of any metal less positive than that used to form the layer of the invention.

5 A tubular cathode containing the active cathode material, silver oxide, conductor and, in some cases, a binder can be inserted so as to engage the inner surface of the container. A separator, suitably made of a non-woven cellulose or polymer fibre, micro- porous plastic or cellophane film, can be lined on the inner surface of the tubular cathode. In this construction the container is in contact with the cathode and, thus, is the positive or o cathodic terminal.
The preferred cathode used in the present invention is a mixture of manganese dioxide, an electrically conductive material and a relatively minor amount of silver oxide. There are many types of suitable conductive materials known. Graphite, synthetic or natural, is preferably used in the cells of the present invention, and is readily commercially 5 available. The cathode can further comprise a binder. Examples of suitable binders include polytetrafluoroethylene and polyethylene. Preferably, the cathodes comprise a major amount of manganese dioxide, a conductive amount of the graphite and a minor amount of silver oxide and often a binding amount of a binder. Typically, the manganese dioxide will comprise between about 80 to 97 weight percent of the total cathode weight. When a binder 0 is employed, the binder will comprise less than about 4% by weight. Silver oxide should be present in the amounts listed above. The remainder of the cathode will be comprised of graphite and electrolyte solution. When the cathode is prepared within the container, the amount of the electrolyte solution added is sufficient to wet the dry components and to provide a mixture than can be moulded. The cathodes are preferably prepared by mixing the 5 components together and dispensing the mix into the container. The mix is then moulded or compressed against the inside of the container. Alternatively, the mix can be pre-moulded as rings and the rings pressed into the container.

The preferred electrolyte used in the present invention is an aqueous alkaline o solution, such a potassium hydroxide or sodium hydroxide. The concentration of the solution can be any concentration that provides for ionic conductivity. In the assembled cell, the concentration of the aqueous alkaline solution ranges from about 30% to about 45%. Alternatively, the electrolyte may be an acidic or a neutral solution.

5 A preferred anode is made of a mixture of active anode material, electrolyte, and, optionally, an electrolyte-swellable binder, such as a polyacrylic acid, which can be enclosed with the separator, separating the cathode from the anode. An anode current collector member is inserted into the anode.
o Preferably, zinc is used as the active anode material in the cells of the invention.

Preferably, the zinc is low gassing zinc and is in powder form. The powdered zinc is combined with a binder and an amount of the electrolyte solution to form a gel. The anode
gel generally expands when it is discharged. Other optional components may also be included in the anode.

It is undesirable for any of the silver compound or silver ions from the silver 5 compound to be in contact with the anode. If silver ions are present, then they can react with the zinc, consuming part of the zinc and generating hydrogen gas. The silver compound and silver ions can be kept out of the anode by allowing sufficient time for all of the soluble silver in the cathode to deposit onto the container wall before the anode is added to the cell and/or by using a separator material, such as cellophane, that will not allow silver 0 ions to pass from the cathode to the anode.

The cell is closed with a cover and sealed. The cover is in electrical contact with the anode current collector member and is the negative or anodic terminal of the cell. Any conventional seal can be employed. It is desired that the cell construction not have a venting 5 means that would freely vent due to the normal pressure generated in the cell during a normal discharge.
The present invention will now be further illustrated with respect to the accompanying drawing, which is a cross-sectional view of an inverted alkaline cell of the o present invention.

In the drawing, the alkaline cell 2 is assembled in a conventional conductive steel container 4, which also forms an external terminal for the cell. The cathode 6 for cell 2 is a mixture of manganese dioxide, silver oxide, graphite, electrolyte and optionally a binder or 5 other additives.

After the cathode 6 is formed in or inserted into the container 4, a separator 8 is added to physically isolate the anode material 10 from the cathode 6 and container 4 while still permitting ion transport between the electrodes. The separator 8 may be made of two o strips of separator material arranged perpendicular to one another and inserted into the cathode's tubular shaped opening, thereby forming a separator basket with a central opening. The anode mix 10 is then added to the separator-lined cavity of the cell. An open
area 12 is left in the cell to provide room for any expansion of the anode mix 10. The anode current collector 22 is located in and protruding from anode mix 10.

To complete assembly of the cell, an external bottom cover 30 is placed into the 5 steel container 4 and is also insulated from contact with the container 4 by the peripheral wall 32 of seal member 34. The bottom cover 30 makes electrical contact with current collector 22, making the bottom cover 30 the external negative terminal for cell 2. The edge of the steel container 4 is rolled to hold the upturned portion 36 of the bottom cover 30 locked in position in the bottom of the cell 2. Top cover 40 can be fastened to the container 0 by welds 42 after the cathode is rammed into place.

As described above, in the preferred embodiment of the invention, silver oxide is a component of the cathode during the cell assembly. After the cathode is formed in the cell or inserted and fixed adjacent to the inside surface of the container 4, the cathode is 5 contacted with electrolyte. The silver oxide or other silver compound is soluble in the electrolyte, dissociates into its ionic components, and diffuses through the cathode to the inside surface of the container 4. As described, the inside surface of the container can be plated or clad with nickel, a nickel cobalt alloy, or bare iron. The silver ions being more positive than the iron, nickel, or cobalt displace these ions and coat the inside surface of the o container. The displacement creates a diffusion potential, which drives further migration towards the inner surface. This process of dissolution, diffusion, and displacement continues until either all the silver from the silver compound is consumed or the cell is discharged. During discharge, the silver oxide is reduced to silver metal and the process is halted. 5

The silver compound can be put into the cell in many ways, depending upon the cell design, cell materials and manufacturing considerations such as convenience, efficiency and the manufacturing process and equipment already being used. For example, powdered silver compound may be mixed with other dry cathode ingredients, followed by addition of o electrolyte, either before or after the other cathode components are put into the container.

Alternatively, the silver compound may be dissolved in electrolyte before it is added to the dry ingredients. Silver compound can also be dissolved in electrolyte which is put into the
container before the cathode or dry cathode ingredients. The precise method or sequence of adding the silver compound is not especially important, except that the silver compound or dissolved silver compound preferably should not come in contact with the anode. This will prevent reaction of the silver ions with the active anode material which would make that silver unavailable for its intended purpose, reduce the discharge capacity of the cell and possibly create undesirable reaction products.

Each of the processes of dissolution, diffusion, and displacement can be accelerated by increasing the temperature. The applicant has found that these processes continue for many hours at ambient temperatures. The cell container is adequately coated in minutes at ambient temperatures; however, the amount of silver accumulated on the container continues to increase. Using heated electrolyte can accelerate the process so that the bulk of the silver accumulates on the container's inner surface in a shorter length of time. Other heating methods or means of accelerating the process are equivalent and will accomplish the same results.

The silver coating on the inner surface acts to enhance electrical contact between the cathode and the container. This coating is formed in situ after the formation of the cathode, and thus is not damaged during cathode formation. The process of formation requires only minimal amounts of silver to be added to the cell, which is more cost effective than prior art coatings. The process of formation does not require any modification in the existing cell construction process. In fact, it allows for the elimination of container cladding, thus resulting in additional cost effectiveness.
EXAMPLE

Several AA SR6 aqueous alkaline cells were produced using a cathode comprising manganese dioxide, graphite and a binder; an anode comprising zinc and an electrolyte of potassium hydroxide solution; and separator; all assembled in steel containers and conductive covers. Cell samples 1 and 10 were prepared as standard. In cell sample 1, the internal wall was uncoated, whereas in cell sample 10, a gold coating was electroplated onto
the inner surface of the cell container. These two standards were thought to represent the boundaries of performance for cathode to container contact. In cell samples 2 and 3, a graphite coating was sprayed onto the inner surface of the cell container. In cell samples 4 and 5, silver was deposited onto the cell container before the cathode was added. In sample 4, silver oxide was added to an alkaline potassium hydroxide solution and allowed to set before the solution was decanted leaving a silver coating on the inner surface of the container. In cell sample 5 silver chloride, a silver halide, was dissolved in an acidic solution and added to the can; after being allowed to set, the solution was decanted. In another sample (not included in the table below), silver nitrate was dissolved in an acidic solution. The silver nitrate, being highly soluble, resulted in a very thick silver coating, which was easily de-laminated and therefore not tested. Samples 6 and 7 were prepared according to the present invention, 0J9 and 0.002 grams of silver oxide were added respectively to the cathode mix. In samples 8 and 9, silver was electroplated onto the cell container at different thicknesses.

The cells were discharged at 2.0 amps to a 1-volt cut-off. The short circuit amperage (S. C. Amp) was measured along with time required for the cell to reach a 1-volt cut-off at a continuous discharge of 2.0 amperes. After testing, the cells were dismantled and the amount of metal deposited on the internal surface of the cell container was measured. This data are shown in the following table.

The data show that the silver coating on the container's wall provided a longer service life than the use of a graphite coating for cell discharged continuously at 2.0 amperes to a 1 volt cut-off.

The data also show that the addition of very small amounts of silver oxide to the cathode mix results in cell performance increases approaching those produced by the electroplated gold reference sample. Though the invention has been described with respect to preferred embodiments thereof, many variations and modifications will become apparent to those skilled in the art. It is therefore the intention that the appended claims be interpreted as broadly as possible in view of the prior art including all such variations and modifications.

claim.claim-text: 1. An assembled, undischarged electrochemical cell comprising electrolyte, an electrode and a container therefor, wherein the surface of the container adjacent the electrode is coated with a layer of a metal which is more electropositive than the metallic material of the container, characterised in that the metal layer is generated by a solute of the metal in the electrolyte.
2. A cell according to claim 1, wherein the metal of the metal layer is silver.
3. A cell according to claim 1 or 2, wherein the solute is a silver compound.

4. A process for the preparation of an electrochemical cell comprising an electrolyte, an electrode and a container therefor made of a metallic material, the process comprising dissolving a compound of a metal more electropositive than the container in the electrolyte in a sufficient quantity that the surface of the container in contact with the electrode becomes coated with the metal by means of an electrochemical equilibrium reaction at the surface of the container.
5. A process according to claim 4, wherein the metal layer replaces at least a portion of the metal of the container wall.
6. A process according to claim 4 or 5, wherein the metal coating the container is silver.
7. A process according to any of claims 4 to 6, wherein the metal compound is a silver compound.
8. A process according to claim 7, wherein the silver compound is a silver oxide.
9. A process according to any of claims 4 to 8, wherein the thickness of the metal coating is between about 0.0001 μm and about 3 μm.

10. A process according to any of claims 4 to 9, wherein the initial amount of metal compound is between about 0.0001 weight percent and about 0.5 weight percent of the active material in the electrode.
11. A process according to claim 10, wherein the amount of metal compound is between about 0.01 weight percent and about 0J weight percent of the active material in the electrode.
12. A process according to any of claims 4 to 11, wherein the metal compound is added to the electrode before the electrode is assembled into the container.
13. A process according to any of claims 4 to 11, wherein the metal compound is dissolved in the electrolyte before the electrolyte is assembled with the electrode in the container.
14. A process according to claim 13, wherein the electrolyte is added to the electrode before the electrode is assembled into the container.
15. A process according to any of claims 4 to 11, wherein the silver compound is added with a liquid to the container and the liquid is removed from the container after the layer of silver is formed.

16. A process according to any of claims 4 to 15, wherein a sufficient amount of metal compound is incorporated into the cell to permit regeneration of the metal coating during the lifetime of the cell.
17. A process according to any of claims 4 to 16, wherein the electrode is a cathode.
18. An electrochemical cell produced using a process according to any of claims 4 to 17.
